newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Chidambaram begins meeting with Left Front.
newsitem.headline: India's Chidambaram begins meeting with Left Front.

text.p: Indian Finance Minister P. Chidambaram began a crucial meeting with heads of left-wing parties on Tuesday to consider their demands for changes in his 1997/98 (April-March) budget, party leaders said.

Leaders of the four parties which make up the Left Front, a powerful bloc within Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's United Front coalition, said they objected to proposals relating to taxes on personal income and dividends, as well as to insurance and duties.
Chidambaram has proposed reducing the tax rate on annual personal income between 40,000 rupees ($1,115) and 60,000 rupees to 10 percent from 15 percent.
The tax rate on income between 60,000 and 150,000 rupees would be cut to 20 percent from 30 percent, while the rate on incomes above 150,000 rupees would be reduced to 30 percent from 40.
Under Chidambaram's path-breaking budget, which has been widely praised by domestic and foreign investors, shareholders also would be exempted from a tax on dividends.

"The highest slab of tax should be 40 percent and the dividend tax should be imposed," Nirmal Kanti Chatterjee, a lawmaker for the Communist Party of India (Marxist), told Reuters as he entered the meeting.
"We are opposed to insurance privatisation, and in customs and excise duties there should be a thorough review," Chatterjee said.
The Left Front comprises the two main communist parties, the Revolutionary Socialist Party and the Forward Bloc.

The lower house of parliament was expected to begin discussion of the Finance Bill, which includes tax and tariff proposals for 1997/98, on Wednesday, and to vote on the package by the end of the week.
Gujral last week promised to hold discussions with major political parties on the budget proposals before parliament voted on the finance bill.
